paragraphs: When the third iron lock fell across the palace gates, Yao Chang was drinking a mouthful of cold tea.

He frowned faintly at the taste. Someone should have been changing the tea in the palace throughout the night, but even the attendants had been sent to the guarded entrances. Clearly Wang Meng’s illness was no longer the night’s only concern.

Under the gallery Murong Chui watched the Feathered Forest Guard change posts without surprise. He had been falsely accused in Yan, had guarded against arrows from behind while leading men into battle, and on the day he fled to Qin he had not even known whether his son would pass the frontier alive. More than once he had felt what it was to have his life balanced on another man’s fingertip.
“Champion General,” Yao Chang said, setting down his cup, “who do you think is to have a bad night?”
“Since you ask, I expect you have already decided.”
“Wang Jinglüe never much cared for men like us. As he prepares to depart, perhaps he means to leave the Heavenly King a list.”
“If my name is on it, yours will not be far behind.”
Yao Chang’s smile stiffened briefly. “Then we shall keep each other company.”

A chamberlain ran through the rain to summon the ministers to Chongde Hall. Their escorts were to remain outside; their swords must be surrendered. Fu Chong was the first to lose his temper. He had carried a blade in the Fu clan’s campaigns from the earliest days. The leather binding on its hilt had worn through several times, and even in sleep he kept it beside his pillow. To have a Feathered Forest captain scarcely out of his teens demand it now was an insult before the entire court.
“Send Fu Rong to me,” the old general roared. “Who dares take my sword?”
The captain’s face went white, but he held his ground. “I carry a written order from the Heavenly King.”

Dozens of guards shifted together along the gallery, the points of their halberds glimmering in the lamplight. Fu Chong gripped his hilt until the veins stood out on his hand. Murong Chui came to his side, unfastened his own short blade, and laid it in the wooden tray.
“Would you truly draw a sword inside the palace?” he asked.
Fu Chong looked sideways at him.
“What if I did?”
“You have already lost two sons on the battlefield,” Murong Chui said evenly. “If you throw away your own life tonight, you will make a bitter mockery of theirs.”
Fu Chong’s hand trembled. At last he flung sword and scabbard into the tray.

One by one the weapons were given up. The bright clang of metal against metal had a chill of its own. Yao Chang surrendered his dagger and attempted a joke: “Once we were told to straighten our robes before meeting the sovereign. Now we must straighten our belts as well.”
No one laughed.

High lamps illuminated Chongde Hall. The curtains had been taken down from all four walls, leaving a long table exposed in the center. Dozens of military registers lay across it, beside an empty wooden chest and several newly cast samples of command tallies. Crown Prince Fu Hong stood below the dais holding an edict. The paper shook faintly in his hands. Fu Rong and Quan Yi stood to either side, their faces grave.
Murong Chui’s gaze settled on the empty chest. He understood. A man could be killed without all these ledgers. To take from him what he had held for years required a far greater apparatus.

Fu Jian entered from a side door. The ministers prostrated themselves, but he did not immediately bid them rise. They had endured a night of wind and rain outside; many robes were still damp. Now, with their foreheads close to the cold tiles, sweat began to gather at their temples.

“An urgent report from Ye,” Fu Jian said. “Weapons and armor have been concealed by former Yan troops. More than thirty-seven hundred households are under suspicion. The affair is still being investigated. There is to be no collective punishment.”

At once a royal kinsman stepped from the ranks and demanded the detention of former Murong officers. Fu Jian ordered him to stand and asked his name, his native place, and the troops he once commanded. The three questions left the man visibly uneasy.
“Among the Di troops you lead, are there comrades from the days when the Fu clan first rose to power?”
“There are, naturally.”
“If one of them plotted rebellion, could I arrest you on that account?”
The man’s face drained of color. “I harbor no such thought!”
“Then on what grounds do you pronounce Murong Chui guilty?”
The ministers exchanged glances. No one else ventured to demand an arrest.

Fu Jian allowed them to rise and motioned for Fu Hong to read the edict. The young crown prince’s voice lacked the deep resonance of the veterans gathered in the hall; after only a few lines sweat stood on his brow. The order concerned an initial audit of the armies stationed around the capital. Tiger tallies held by royal kinsmen and commanders of former tribal forces were to be deposited temporarily with the Department of State Affairs. Within three days, actual troop strengths, provisions, pay, and chains of command would be checked, and commissions reissued accordingly. Military households were neither to move without permission nor to have their property seized under the pretext of inspection.
“I will not accept it!”
Fu Chong was the first to step forward.

His hair was white, old sword scars cut deep across his face, and his voice carried a strange, wounded grandeur. “I led these men before Your Majesty ascended the throne. We fought for Guanzhong and Bingzhou together. And now one edict is enough to take them from me? Has Your Majesty asked whom they believe they are fighting for?”
Many heads remained lowered. Fu Chong had asked the question for himself, and for the rest of them.
“I have,” Fu Jian said. “Tell me first: what do the men in your camp eat?”
“Army grain.”
“And where does it come from?”
“The court granaries.”
“Who feeds their wives and children when they die in battle?”
“The army administration provides relief.”
“And if the money and grain allotted for them are diverted along the way by their own commanders?”
Fu Chong started. “I would never do such a thing!”
“I did not say you would. I want to know whom a soldier can turn to besides Fu Chong.”

The old general had no answer. His men knew his standard; they knew the two sons he had buried. He had pleaded for rewards on behalf of his comrades, sought grain for widows, and gone in person to curse officers who made unjust demands. But ask who would undertake those duties after his death, and he could name no one he trusted to do it.
“Your Majesty,” he said more quietly, “they have followed me for decades.”

“I know.” Fu Jian descended from the dais. “That is why I ask you today for the tally that commands them. As for who should receive grain, who should be cared for when wounded or dead—you will account for every man with the Department of State Affairs. I mean them to have a chance of surviving in their own camps even when you are gone.”
Fu Chong raised his head defiantly. “And if I refuse?”
Fu Jian gave no reply. He unfastened a black Central Army tally from his own belt and placed it in the chest.
After that small sound, the hall grew so quiet that even the breathing of the men could be heard.
“Mine goes in as well.”

Fu Jian pushed the chest into the middle of the table and ordered Quan Yi to affix the seals. One gesture could not strip every commander of his personal following, but it showed them that the emperor was willing to make the first incision in his own flesh.

Quan Yi seized the moment to present a document from the Granary Office. Never fond of abstract debate, he began with numbers of men and measures of grain. “There is a difficulty I must ask Your Majesty to settle. Yesterday the Feathered Forest Guard changed stations. The palace issued an order; the military office received a tally; but the granary officials did not know what would authorize them to release provisions. One lowly clerk was so afraid of being punished that he embraced the storehouse keys and refused to open the door.”
“What happened then?” Fu Jian asked.

“I made all three offices furnish written attestations. Only then would he open up. If anyone uses an edict tomorrow to move troops, the Granary Office will still not dare rely on one piece of paper.”
Some of the ministers, so tense a moment earlier, almost smiled. Fu Jian instead took the three documents, studied them one by one, and called Fu Rong forward to deliberate.

“Let us establish a provisional procedure tonight,” he said. “The Secretariat issues the edict; the Central Army Office verifies the troops; the Department of State Affairs releases grain against the actual registers. We shall try it around the capital for three months. In an emergency on the frontier, one battalion may march on urgent orders and supply the missing attestations afterward. Large deployments to the north or south may not proceed without all three offices completing their part.”
Quan Yi wrote down every word. His brush stopped at the final line. “What if the three offices cannot agree?”
“They may come to me.”
“And if Your Majesty is determined to send the army regardless?”
Fu Jian looked at him for a long time. “Then the realm must at least know that the decision was mine alone.”
Quan Yi lifted his eyes and held his brush motionless. Fu Jian tapped the edge of the table, telling him to write it exactly so.
“Your Majesty,” Yao Chang said suddenly, leaving his place and kneeling before the long table, “I am wholly persuaded that the armies should obey one command. I am willing to surrender my tally.”

He offered it with both hands. His thumb lingered on the bronze knob, though his voice remained mild. Fu Jian ordered it taken, then announced before the assembled ministers that the Qiang forces of the Yao family would be divided into several commands under newly appointed officers. Yao Chang would remain in Chang’an as General of the Right Guard, no longer visiting the Qiang country in person to command or pacify its settlements.
Yao Chang bowed his forehead to the floor. A cord of muscle jumped sharply at the back of his neck.
“There are old feuds among the Qiang,” he said, raising his head and choosing his words carefully. “I fear that a sudden change of commanders may bring disorder to the frontier.”
“So do I.”
A flicker of hope came into Yao Chang’s eyes.

“Which is why we shall separate the registers first and leave the garrisons where they are for now. You know the Qiang country. Draw up the defensive maps for their new commanders.” Fu Jian held his gaze. “Explain them well enough that they need not summon you back just to keep the passes.”
“I ... obey.”

Yao Chang surrendered the tiger tally. When his fingers opened, two angry red marks remained across his palm. He returned to his place in the ranks with the same agreeable expression and even breathing, but he did not look at Fu Jian again.
“Murong Chui.”
The Champion General stepped from the ranks, his armor giving a soft metallic whisper.
“Your Majesty.”
Fu Jian faced him. “What do you think of tonight’s edict?”

Murong Chui did not rush to flatter him. In Yan he had led tens of thousands of armored horsemen. He knew how much a familiar banner, an accent, and a single trusted commander mattered when battle dissolved into confusion. To separate those ties by collecting tallies in one night might prove harder than taking a fortified city.
“If Your Majesty wants the truth, I have three concerns.”
“Speak.”

“Change a frontier army’s commander overnight, and if raiders come the new man will not know the country well enough to act. Leave every register to clerks in the capital, and when a distant supply road is closed for three months the troops cannot wait for permission written on silk. And if we mix the men of the tribes and the Han, we must remember that archers, horsemen, infantry, heavy armor, and light armor have different ways of fighting. We cannot simply divide them by surname.”

Several commanders who had been ready to protest nodded vigorously. Fu Rong looked up; Quan Yi ceased writing for a moment. Everything Murong Chui had said described a genuine difficulty. Not one sentence defended his personal right to command his old soldiers.
“Have you a solution?” Fu Jian asked.

“Train a single battalion around the capital first,” Murong Chui replied. “Choose officers for ability, and assign the men according to what their drills show. Commanders must receive their commissions anew from the military office; the dependents of the old units need their own accurate household rolls. Go more slowly on the frontier, garrison by garrison. We may see something workable in three months; three years may not be enough to finish the task.”
Fu Jian listened without interruption.
“You have given the matter some thought.”
“I command soldiers. If an army falls apart, the common men die first.”

“Very well.” Fu Jian came down from the dais. “Remain with the Central Army Office and direct the trial reorganization. Surrender your former Yan formations. In their place I shall appoint you over a mixed force of thirty thousand men. Its provisions, pay, movements, rewards, and punishments will follow the new regulations. Censors and military officers will inspect the camps. Make this force work, and you may train it. Fail, and the military administration will choose another commander.”
A murmur of astonishment passed through the hall.
For the first time Murong Chui’s expression changed. “Your Majesty still dares entrust soldiers to me?”
“I have need of your abilities.”
“And if I try to take them away?”
“Try.”

Murong Chui gazed at the emperor. He had expected, at best, a comfortable office without command; at worst, poison in a palace cup. Instead Fu Jian was setting another perilous wager before him in front of the whole court. His old Yan men would no longer follow his word alone, yet Qin would still let him command troops—and require him to prove himself by deeds.
“Does Lord Wang know of this?” he asked.

“At this moment Jinglüe merely hopes I will make fewer mistakes.” Fu Jian paused. “I know he does not trust you. Nor can I return your former army merely because I do. From now on, obey military law and I shall judge you by military law. If you are guilty, I will not pardon you. If someone accuses you without evidence, I will not permit that either.”
At those last words, Murong Chui slowly bowed to the floor.
“I accept the command.”

He drew out the tiger tally. Years of handling had worn its bronze edges smooth. He remembered the snow in the old Xianbei camps, the veterans who had charged with him below the Yan Mountains, the banners he had left behind when he fled defeat. Holding the tally flat in his hand, he found himself reluctant to let it go.
Fu Jian held out his own hand and took it.
“Does it pain you?”
“It does.”
“Anything more?”
“Only this: if men die in the trial battalion, do not let them die for nothing.”
Fu Jian closed his fingers around the tally. “Record every casualty by name, and compensate the families according to the rolls. Quan Yi, add that provision.”

The tally fell into the chest, which was growing heavy now. Other commanders came forward in turn, some readily, some hesitantly, some gripping their bronze tallies until their palms bled. Fu Chong was the last to leave the ranks.

He knelt before the table with his tally in his hand, but he looked directly at Fu Jian. “I lost one son in Bingzhou and the other in Hedong. Many of the young men in my camp grew up alongside them. I promised their mothers I would bring as many home as I could.”
Fu Jian came down the steps and supported him by his crippled leg.
“You can still care for them, old general.”
“But the decisions will no longer be mine.”
“Nor should you have to carry every one of their lives alone.”

Fu Chong bowed his head. He sat motionless for a long while, then opened his hand. The bronze struck the other tallies at the bottom of the chest with a deep, dull sound, like old armor falling from a great height.

Quan Yi counted each tally and checked it against the registers. Fu Hong recorded the military rolls and granary accounts that each command must submit; as he wrote, his brush strokes grew steadier. Outside, the storm was passing, but everyone present knew that the storms of the coming months had only begun.

Fu Jian ordered the generals to remain in the palace overnight. Urgent official documents must be presented to him for inspection; private letters could not leave for the time being, nor could troops be moved without authorization. Some grumbled, but Yao Chang was again the first to assent, leaving the others with little room to object.
As they left the hall, Murong Chui and Yao Chang met at the end of the long corridor. Yao Chang bowed. His smile was as polished as ever.
“My congratulations, Champion General. One night you lose your old army, and the next you gain thirty thousand new men.”
“You will remain in Chang’an, closer to the Heavenly King. I would not call that a disaster either.”
A faint ripple crossed Yao Chang’s eyes. “Must you mock me, General?”
“I am only telling the truth.”

They looked at one another once more. Beyond the window the palace lamps rocked in the wind, throwing light and shadow across the rain-slick stones. Murong Chui was the first to leave. Yao Chang lingered, then raised his sleeve to his mouth and gave a quiet cough. No one could say what he was thinking. Farther down the gallery, the newly posted Feathered Forest Guards no longer recognized the old badges of the Qiang camps.
When Fu Jian returned to Chengming Hall, Wang Meng was still awake. The medicine beside the bed had gone cold; a little red blossom of spent wick had formed on the candle.
“The generals have surrendered their tallies.” Fu Jian sat and kept his voice as light as he could. “You always say I postpone the hard things. I did not postpone this one.”
“Who ... was hardest?” Wang Meng asked.
“Fu Chong could scarcely part with his old soldiers. Yao Chang agreed with suspicious speed. Murong Chui argued with me half the night and offered a good many practical suggestions.”
A small light came into Wang Meng’s eyes, then faded.
“What did Your Majesty give him to do?”
“Train the new mixed army.”
Wang Meng watched him for a long time. His lips moved almost imperceptibly.
“Of course.”

Fu Jian knew what would come next. He took Wang Meng’s hand before the sick man could speak. “Jinglüe, I have not returned the old Yan army to him. There are officers to check the pay, registers, and tallies. If the court dares employ only mediocre commanders, the new army will be just another body of men waiting to be cut down.”
“I fear ...”
“So do I.” Fu Jian interrupted gently. “But someone must mount the horse and try.”

Wang Meng closed his eyes for a long time. He had no strength left to argue with the emperor. His fingertip merely traced a few faint strokes against Fu Jian’s palm, as though he were still writing an unfinished military order.
“Do not hurry ... to Hebei.”
“The capital first, then Hedong. If it fails, we change it.”
“The soldiers' pay ...”
“Will be audited.”
“Their families ... the men killed ...”
“Relief, from verified rolls.”
Wang Meng nodded faintly, then opened his eyes again. “And Hong?”

“He has spent the entire night recording accounts in Chongde Hall. He copied two lines incorrectly, scraped them clean, and wrote them again. When you are well, I shall send him with the ledgers for you to teach him.”

Wang Meng gave the faintest laugh. He wanted to say that the crown prince must learn more than kindness and more than the power to decide with a single blow. He must learn, when everyone waited for him to speak, to understand first what he had not yet understood. But Wang Meng could no longer gather enough breath to finish the thought.
Fu Jian bent closer. “Jinglüe, what else is there for you to teach me?”
Beyond the paper windows, the rain stopped.

Wang Meng looked at Fu Jian with sudden tenderness. After all these years, the man before him still possessed the same youthful refusal to yield. Fu Jian could pardon enemies, receive strangers of other peoples, and imagine an empire large enough to hold them all. For those very reasons, he could never quite believe that some matters must be left to another day, or that some men must be held in check by law. To halt his horse tonight had cost him nearly every ounce of strength he possessed.
With great effort, Wang Meng turned his hand palm down and rested it on the back of Fu Jian’s.
“Go slowly.”
Fu Jian’s eyes burned.
“I will.”
Wang Meng’s gaze remained on his face, then slowly lost its focus. Fu Jian waited a long time and called Jinglüe twice, softly. No reply came. The fingers in his hand did not tighten again.
Another quarter sounded from the palace water clock.
Fu Jian remained seated. It was as though, if he refused to release the hand, Wang Meng might still open his eyes at the next difficulty and tell him, with his old impatience, what must be done.
Only when the dawn turned gray did he reach out, straighten Wang Meng’s collar, and put the exposed hand back beneath the embroidered coverlet.
“I took back the tiger tallies,” he whispered.

Only after speaking did he grasp how much remained. Men would still refuse to yield the rolls; others could still call their old followers together on the frontier; countless eyes were turned toward Chang’an, waiting for him to make one mistake. The bronze and iron recovered tonight weighed little beside the burdens Wang Meng had borne for him while alive.
The doors opened. Fu Rong, Quan Yi, and Fu Hong had kept watch outside. When they saw the stains of medicine on the emperor’s robe and the exhaustion around his eyes, all three sank to their knees.
Fu Jian steadied himself against the doorframe, faced the chill wind after the rain, and said in a low, clear voice: “Grand Commandant Wang Meng is dead.”

The mourning bell sounded from the palace tower, stroke after stroke carrying beyond the vermilion walls into the southern wards and northern barracks. Shopkeepers opened their doors, unsure whose death had called forth such bells. But the generals confined within the palace understood. Murong Chui sat in the eastern wing, watching the windows brighten in silence. Yao Chang rose and poured onto the floor the cold tea he had not touched all night. Fu Chong no longer wore his tally at his waist, yet his hand still rested in the place where it had hung.

Morning light fell across the long table in Chongde Hall. The clay seal on the wooden chest had not yet dried. Inside, dozens of bronze and iron tallies lay like dead things. Outside, the hearts of living men would find no easy sleep after that night.

The morning drums sounded. Outside Chongde Hall a junior granary clerk was already waiting with the new army’s provision ledger in his arms. He stood awkwardly, unsure whether to ask first about last night’s edict or offer condolences for the Grand Commandant.
Fu Hong passed along the corridor, saw the clerk, and reached out to take the ledger.
